meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Setting off — to school, to work, to the market.

senses.def: to go (somewhere): ذَهَبَ إِلَى … (to go to …)
to go away, to leave, to be gone
ذَهَبَ إِلَى أَنَّ … — to hold the view that … (formal)

examples.tr: I go to school on foot.
Where are you going? (to a woman)
Go to your room!
The train has gone.

examples.text: ذَهَبَ بَعْضُ الْعُلَمَاءِ إِلَى أَنَّ هٰذَا الرَّأْيَ خَطَأٌ.
examples.tr: Some scholars held that this view is wrong.

collocations.tr: to take … away, to take … along (Wiktionary)

synonyms.nuance: to go on, to pass (also of time)
the everyday “go” of Levantine and Egyptian Arabic

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root ذ ه ب (non-past يَذْهَبُ, verbal noun ذَهَاب) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same three letters spell ذَهَب, “gold”: an unvocalized ذهب can be “he went” or “gold”.
The Arabic title of Gone with the Wind is ذهب مع الريح.
pitfalls: The present has a: يَذْهَبُ (not *يَذْهُبُ), so the imperative starts with i: اِذْهَبْ!
The goal takes إِلَى: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ — never فِي (Greek σε, German in/zu are both إِلَى here).
subtleties: ذَهَبَ is “go” however you go — on foot or by car; German gehen / fahren are both ذَهَبَ (the vehicle comes with بِـ: ذَهَبْتُ بِالْقِطَارِ).

governs.what: the place (or a direct object: جَاءَ الْبَيْتَ)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

contrasts.value: to come (all forms but the imperative)

profile.feeling: Someone arriving where you are — guests, the bus, the winter.

senses.def: to occur, to be (in a text): جَاءَ فِي الْكِتَابِ … (it says in the book …)

examples.tr: My father comes home from work in the evening.
When are you coming? (to a woman)
Winter has come.
He brought the book.

synonyms.nuance: to come — frequent in writing and in the Qurʾān (present يَأْتِي)
to come, to attend, to be present (at a meeting, a lesson)

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root ج ي ء, hollow and with a final hamza (non-past يَجِيءُ, verbal noun مَجِيء) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its imperative جِئْ is hardly used: “come!” is تَعَالَ, which Wiktionary describes as the form replacing the awkward imperatives of جَاءَ.
pitfalls: Hollow verb: long ā in جَاءَ (he came), long ī in the present يَجِيءُ, short i in جِئْتُ (I came).
The hamza changes its seat: جَاءَ, جِئْتُ, يَجِيئُونَ, جَاؤُوا.
subtleties: Like English, Arabic separates ذَهَبَ (go, away from here) and جَاءَ (come, towards the speaker); Greek έρχομαι = جَاءَ.

present.none: an imperative only; the verb تَعَالَى (يَتَعَالَى) means “to be exalted”

masdar.none: an imperative only: no maṣdar of its own

governs.what: the place or the person (تَعَالَ إِلَيَّ)

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: A wave of the hand: “come here!”.

senses.def: come (here)! — the imperative that serves جَاءَ

examples.tr: Come here! (to a man)
Come with me! (to a woman)
Come to the kitchen! (to several people)

synonyms.nuance: come on!, come here! — classical

etymology.text: The imperative of تَعَالَى (form VI of the root ع ل و); Wiktionary: it supplies the imperative of جَاءَ, whose own imperative forms are phonetically impractical.

funFacts: Its root ع ل و is the root of عَلَى (on) and عَالٍ (high).
The colloquial forms of “come!” all go back to it.
pitfalls: Only a command: there is no past or present “he comes” from تَعَالَ — use جَاءَ / يَجِيءُ.
Endings of a weak verb: تَعَالَ (to a man), تَعَالَيْ (to a woman), تَعَالَوْا (to several); in speech one also hears taʿāli to a woman.
subtleties: It is used everywhere, from classical texts to the street, and is never rude — unlike اُخْرُجْ! (get out!).

governs.what: the place walked to (مَشَى إِلَى الْبَيْتِ)

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Footsteps: a walk in the park, walking to work.

senses.def: to walk, to go on foot

examples.tr: I walk to work.
We walk in the park in the evening.
Walk slowly!

collocations.tr: to walk, to go on foot

synonyms.nuance: to go, to move along, to walk — written style
to stroll, to take a walk for pleasure

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root م ش ي (non-past يَمْشِي, verbal noun مَشْي) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its verbal noun in the accusative, مَشْيًا, is the Arabic “on foot”.
pitfalls: Final weak y: يَمْشِي (he walks), but the imperative to a man loses it: اِمْشِ!
تَمْشِينَ is both “you (one woman) walk” and “you (women) walk”.
subtleties: مَشَى is walking as a way of moving; “go somewhere” is ذَهَبَ: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ مَشْيًا = I go to work on foot.

governs.what: the place run to (رَكَضَ إِلَى الْبَابِ)

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Hurry and breath: children running, running for the bus.

examples.tr: The child is running in the garden.
I run every morning.
Run! The train is here.

synonyms.nuance: to run — also “to flow, to happen”; the everyday word in Egypt (يَجْرِي)
to run, to race (عَدَّاء = runner)

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root ر ك ض (non-past يَرْكُضُ); Wiktionary compares Classical Syriac ܪܗܛ, Hebrew רָץ (rats) and Geʿez ሮጸ (roṣä).

funFacts: Wiktionary compares it with Hebrew רָץ (rats, “runs”).
pitfalls: The present has u: يَرْكُضُ, so the imperative starts with u: اُرْكُضْ!
subtleties: رَكَضَ is the standard written word; in Egyptian speech people say جَرَى / يَجْرِي.

governs.what: people, an army, a team (قَادَ الْفَرِيقَ)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Hands on the wheel — and, in a bigger sense, leading people.

senses.def: to lead, to guide, to command

examples.tr: My father is driving the car.
Do you drive (a car)? (to a woman)
Drive slowly!
He led the army.

synonyms.nuance: to drive (a car) — common in Egypt and in speech; also “to drive (animals)”

etymology.text: Form I verb of the hollow root ق و د (non-past يَقُودُ, verbal noun قِيَادَة or قَوْد); Wiktionary: to lead, to steer, to drive, to guide, to rule.

funFacts: قَائِد (leader, commander) and قِيَادَة (leadership; driving) share the root: رُخْصَةُ قِيَادَةٍ is a driving licence.
pitfalls: Hollow verb: ā in قَادَ, ū in يَقُودُ, short u in قُدْتُ (I drove) and in the command قُدْ!
The women forms keep the short u: تَقُدْنَ, يَقُدْنَ.
subtleties: قَادَ takes the vehicle as object (قَادَ السَّيَّارَةَ); “go by car” is ذَهَبَ بِالسَّيَّارَةِ — German fahren covers both.

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Suitcases, tickets and distant cities.

senses.def: to travel, to go on a journey

examples.tr: I travel to Egypt in the summer.
My brother travels by plane.
Travel with us! (to a woman)

phrases.tr: travel is a piece of torment

synonyms.nuance: to depart, to set out on a journey (رِحْلَة = trip)

etymology.text: Form III verb of the root س ف ر (non-past يُسَافِرُ, verbal noun مُسَافَرَة or سَفَر); Wiktionary compares سَفَر (journey, travel).

funFacts: Swahili safari (journey) comes from Arabic سَفَر — and English took safari from Swahili.
مُسَافِر is a traveller or a passenger.
pitfalls: Form III: u in the present prefix (أُسَافِرُ, يُسَافِرُ) and i before the last root letter.
The past has a long ā: سَافَرْتُ (I travelled), not *سَفَرْتُ.
subtleties: سَافَرَ is a journey to another town or country; for the daily way to work use ذَهَبَ.

governs.what: a present verb after لَمْ: no longer (لَمْ يَعُدْ يَسْكُنُ هُنَا)

meaningForms.what: the maṣdar of this meaning (visiting the sick)

profile.feeling: Coming home: the way back.

senses.def: to return, to go back, to come back
to do again; لَمْ يَعُدْ … = no longer …
to visit (a sick person) — a separate word with the same letters

examples.tr: I go back home in the evening.
When do you come back from work?
Come back quickly!
The doctor visited the sick man.
We visited my grandfather in hospital.
He no longer lives here.

synonyms.nuance: to return — the more common word in speech (رِجِع)
to return, to come back (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Form I verb of the hollow root ع و د (non-past يَعُودُ, verbal noun عَوْدَة or عَوْد); Wiktionary: to return, to go back, to come back; to do again.

funFacts: Arab lexicographers derive عِيد (feast) from this root: the day that comes back every year.
pitfalls: Hollow verb like قَادَ: يَعُودُ, عُدْتُ (I came back), عُدْ! (come back!).
subtleties: One verb for both directions: عَادَ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ is “go back home” or “come back home” — Greek γυρίζω also covers both.

governs.what: the place (دَخَلَ الْغُرْفَةَ; also with إِلَى)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: A door opening: going in, coming in.

senses.def: to enter, to go in, to come in
to take up, to start (a school, a profession)

examples.tr: We go into the house.
The teacher came into the classroom.
Come in, please!
My sister started university.

synonyms.nuance: to enter, to penetrate — classical style

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root د خ ل (non-past يَدْخُلُ, verbal noun دُخُول) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: مَدْخَل is an entrance and دَخْل an income — what comes in.
pitfalls: Usually with a direct object, no preposition: دَخَلْتُ الْغُرْفَةَ (I entered the room); دَخَلَ إِلَى … is also correct.
The present has u, so the imperative starts with u: اُدْخُلْ!
subtleties: To invite someone in, تَفَضَّلْ (please, come in) is more polite than the bare imperative اُدْخُلْ.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Stepping outside: out of the house, out with friends.

senses.def: to go out, to leave (a place): خَرَجَ مِنْ …

examples.tr: I leave the house in the morning.
The girl comes out of school at noon.
We go out with friends.
Get out of here!

collocations.tr: to go out of …, to leave …

synonyms.nuance: to leave, to depart from (a place) — with a direct object
to go out (Levant, Egypt); in standard Arabic “to rise, to go up”

etymology.text: From the root خ ر ج; Wiktionary: ultimately from Iranian — see خَرَاج (ḫarāj, “poll-tax”). Form I (non-past يَخْرُجُ, verbal noun خُرُوج).

funFacts: مَخْرَج is an exit (on signs), and مُخْرِج (from form IV) a film director — the one who “brings out” the film.
pitfalls: “Leave a place” needs مِنْ: خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ — or use غَادَرَ with a direct object: غَادَرْتُ الْبَيْتَ.
The imperative اُخْرُجْ! sounds rude (“get out!”).
subtleties: خَرَجَ is movement from inside to outside (go out); غَادَرَ is leaving a place behind (depart).

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Departure boards and announcements.

senses.def: to leave, to depart from (a place) — with a direct object

examples.text: يُغَادِرُ الْقِطَارُ الْمَحَطَّةَ فِي السَّاعَةِ السَّابِعَةِ.
examples.tr: The train leaves the station at seven o’clock.
We left the hotel in the morning.
Leave the building, please!

synonyms.nuance: to go out of — the everyday way to say “leave”
to depart, to set out

etymology.text: Form III verb of the root غ د ر (non-past يُغَادِرُ, verbal noun مُغَادَرَة); Wiktionary: to leave.

funFacts: At airports: الْمُغَادَرَةُ (departures) and الْوُصُولُ (arrivals) — the verbal nouns of غَادَرَ and وَصَلَ.
pitfalls: Transitive: غَادَرَ الْبَيْتَ — no مِنْ (unlike خَرَجَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ).
Form III: u in the present prefix: يُغَادِرُ, أُغَادِرُ.
subtleties: More formal than خَرَجَ: news, timetables, announcements. Form I of the same root, غَدَرَ, means “to betray”.

governs.what: the place reached (also a direct object: وَصَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ)
one thing to another (وَصَلَ الشَّيْءَ بِالشَّيْءِ); also بَيْنَ

profile.feeling: The end of the journey: “we’re here!”.

senses.def: to arrive (at), to reach: وَصَلَ إِلَى …
to join, to connect (a separate entry in Wiktionary)

examples.tr: The train arrives in the evening.
When do you arrive at the airport? (to a woman)
We’ve arrived!

examples.text: يَصِلُ هٰذَا الْجِسْرُ بَيْنَ ضِفَّتَيِ النَّهْرِ.
examples.tr: This bridge connects the two banks of the river.

synonyms.nuance: to reach, to attain (a place, an age, a goal)

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root و ص ل (non-past يَصِلُ); Wiktionary has two entries: “to unite, to join” and “to arrive at, to reach”.

funFacts: وُصُول is arrival; إِيصَال a receipt; صِلَة a link — all from this root.
pitfalls: Assimilated verb: the w drops in the present — يَصِلُ, أَصِلُ, تَصِلِينَ (not *يَوْصِلُ).
With a place: وَصَلَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ, or directly وَصَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ.
subtleties: Greek φτάνω, German ankommen: Arabic says وَصَلَ + إِلَى. Its command form صِلْ! is rarely needed.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Not moving: staying at home, staying with someone.

examples.tr: I’m staying at home today.
My mother stayed with the children.
Stay here!
A little bread is left.

phrases.meaning: said to offer condolences after a death

synonyms.nuance: to remain, to keep (doing)
to stay, to linger
to stay (Egypt, the Gulf); in standard Arabic “to sit”

etymology.text: Form I verb of the root ب ق ي (non-past يَبْقَى, verbal noun بَقَاء); Wiktionary: to last, to endure; to stay, to remain.

funFacts: بَقَاء is survival: الْبَقَاءُ لِلْأَصْلَحِ = the survival of the fittest.
pitfalls: Past with i, present with a: بَقِيَ → يَبْقَى (written with ى).
The imperative loses the last letter: اِبْقَ! (to a woman اِبْقَيْ!); “they stay” is يَبْقَوْنَ (-awna), not *يَبْقُونَ.
subtleties: Also “to be left”: بَقِيَ لِي يَوْمَانِ = I have two days left.

governs.what: the person or thing waited for (اِنْتَظَرَ الْحَافِلَةَ)

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Bus stops and waiting rooms.

senses.def: to wait (for), to await — with a direct object

examples.tr: I’m waiting for the bus.
We’re waiting for you at the café.
Wait a moment!

synonyms.nuance: to await, to look forward to (anxiously)

etymology.text: Form VIII (اِفْتَعَلَ) verb of the root ن ظ ر, “to look” (non-past يَنْتَظِرُ, verbal noun اِنْتِظَار); Wiktionary: to wait for, to await.

funFacts: The root of “looking”: نَظَّارَة (glasses) and مَنْظَر (view) belong to it too.
pitfalls: Transitive, no preposition: أَنْتَظِرُ أَخِي (I’m waiting for my brother), not *أَنْتَظِرُ لِأَخِي.
The first alif is hamzat al-waṣl: at the start اِنْتَظِرْ!, after a vowel silent: وَانْتَظَرَ.
subtleties: Like Greek περιμένω and unlike German warten auf, it takes a direct object.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Bus stops, crowds and timetables.

examples.tr: I go to work by bus.

Where is the bus stop?

examples.text: قَدْ تَعْنِي الْحَافِلَةُ فِي الْمَعَاجِمِ التِّرَامَ أَيْضًا.
examples.tr: In dictionaries, ḥāfila can also mean a tram.

synonyms.nuance: bus — from English, the everyday word in the Levant and the Gulf
bus — Egypt, from French autobus

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a tool noun from the active participle of حَفَلَ (ḥafala, “to gather”) — حَافِل (“gatherer”) + ـَة.

funFacts: Literally “the gatherer”: حَفْلَة (party) and اِحْتِفَال (celebration) come from the same root of gathering.
pitfalls: “By bus” is بِالْحَافِلَةِ, with the article.
Plural حَافِلَات (Wiktionary also gives حَوَافِل).
subtleties: حَافِلَة is the word of signs, news and textbooks; most people say بَاص (Levant, Gulf) or أُوتُوبِيس (Egypt).

meaningForms.none: no other form belongs to one meaning (the plurals do: see plurals)

contrasts.value: a line of camels, one behind the other

profile.feeling: Platforms, rails and long journeys.

senses.def: row; a line of camels (the old meaning)

examples.tr: We travel by train.
The train arrives at eight o’clock.
We saw a line of camels.

profile.synonymsNone: There is no other common word: قِطَار is the train everywhere.

etymology.text: From the root ق ط ر; Wiktionary gives the meanings “row”, “row of camels” and “train” — the train is named after a caravan in a line.

funFacts: The train borrowed the name of the camel caravan walking in single file.
pitfalls: Masculine, but with a feminine-looking plural: قِطَارَات (Wiktionary also gives قُطُر).
subtleties: “By train” is بِالْقِطَارِ; “the train station” مَحَطَّةُ الْقِطَارِ (lesson 11).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses طَائِرَة as “airplane” — the course concept “plane”; the check does not find the word “plane” inside “airplane”.

profile.feeling: Airports, holidays, far-away places.

examples.tr: I travel by plane.
The plane arrives in the evening.
The children are playing with a kite.

synonyms.nuance: plane — the spoken word in many countries

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from the root ط ي ر (ṭ y r), related to flying — the feminine of طَائِر (flying; a bird).

funFacts: Literally “the flying one”: طَائِر is a bird and طَيَّار a pilot.
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat after ā: طَائِرَة (ṭāʾira).
subtleties: A plane is feminine like most vehicles in -a: سَيَّارَة, حَافِلَة, دَرَّاجَة, سَفِينَة.

root.none: a phrase: سَيَّارَة (س ي ر) + أُجْرَة (ء ج ر)

pattern.none: a phrase: each word has its own measure

plurals.note: the head noun takes the plural: سَيَّارَاتُ أُجْرَةٍ

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: A raised hand at the kerb, a fare to agree on.

examples.tr: I go to the airport by taxi.

The taxi driver is nice.

synonyms.nuance: taxi — from French; what almost everyone says
a shared taxi on a fixed route (Levant)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from سَيَّارَة (car) + أُجْرَة (rent, fare, wages) — “a car for hire”.

funFacts: أُجْرَة alone is the fare or the wage: كَمِ الْأُجْرَةُ؟ — how much is the fare?
pitfalls: Two words in a construct: only the first one takes the case ending and it never takes the article: سَيَّارَةُ أُجْرَةٍ, سَيَّارَةُ الْأُجْرَةِ (the taxi); plural سَيَّارَاتُ أُجْرَةٍ.
subtleties: In speech almost everyone says تَاكْسِي; سَيَّارَةُ أُجْرَةٍ is the written and formal word.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Traffic, roads, family trips.

examples.tr: We have a new car.
I go to work by car.
And there came a caravan (Qurʾān 12:19)

synonyms.nuance: car — the everyday word in Egypt

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a tool noun from the characteristic adjective of سَارَ (sāra, “to move, to travel”) — سَيَّار (“moving frequently”) + ـَة.

funFacts: In old Arabic سَيَّارَة was a caravan (Qurʾān 12:19); the old word was given the new meaning “car” in modern times.
كَوْكَبٌ سَيَّارٌ, a “wandering star”, is a planet (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The y is doubled: sayyāra, سَيَّارَة.
subtleties: Feminine: سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ, سَيَّارَتِي (my car).

profile.feeling: Pedals, bells and a ride in the park.

senses.def: دَرَّاجَةٌ نَارِيَّةٌ — motorcycle (lit. a fire bike)

examples.tr: My brother goes to school by bike.
I have an old bike.
He rode a motorbike.

synonyms.nuance: bicycle — from French bicyclette (Levant)
bicycle in Egypt; in standard Arabic “wheel”

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from the root د ر ج (d r j) — a tool noun from دَرَجَ (daraja, “to proceed gradually”).

funFacts: Same root as دَرَج (stairs, lesson 12) and دَرَجَة (step, degree): moving step by step.
pitfalls: The r is doubled: darrāja.
subtleties: دَرَّاجَة alone is usually the bicycle; to be clear: دَرَّاجَةٌ هَوَائِيَّةٌ (bicycle) vs دَرَّاجَةٌ نَارِيَّةٌ (motorbike).

profile.feeling: The sea, ports, long crossings.

examples.tr: We went to the island by ship.
The ship is in the port.
Noah’s ark

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from Aramaic סְפינִתָּא (sǝp̄īntā), forming the root س ف ن; cognate with Hebrew סְפִינָה (sᵊfīnāh).

funFacts: Hebrew סְפִינָה (sfina) is the same word.
سَفِينَةُ الصَّحْرَاءِ, “the ship of the desert”, is the camel.
pitfalls: Broken plural سُفُن (sufun).
subtleties: سَفِينَة is a ship; a small boat is قَارِب — together they cover the course word “boat, ship”.

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Fishermen, rivers and small harbours.

examples.tr: The fisherman’s boat is small.
We crossed the river in a boat.
There are many boats on the lake.

synonyms.nuance: a small boat, a skiff
a boat or vessel of any size

etymology.text: Wiktionary: perhaps from the active participle of قَرِبَ (“to come near”) — a small boat used to approach the shore; alternatively a loan from Latin carabus or Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos).

funFacts: If it comes from Greek κάραβος, it is a cousin of Modern Greek καράβι (ship).
pitfalls: The plural قَوَارِبُ is diptote (no tanwīn): قَوَارِبُ كَثِيرَةٌ.
Do not confuse قَارِب (boat) with قَرِيب (near, lesson 12) and أَقَارِب (relatives).
subtleties: قَارِب is small (rowing, fishing); a big ship is سَفِينَة or بَاخِرَة.

features.derivedFrom: مَشْي (walking), the maṣdar of مَشَى, in the accusative

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Walking instead of riding.

examples.tr: I go to school on foot.
The station is near, we’ll go on foot.
They arrived on foot.

collocations.tr: on foot (lit. walking on the feet)

synonyms.nuance: on foot — the style of the news
on foot (lit. on the feet)

etymology.text: The accusative of مَشْي, the verbal noun of مَشَى (“to walk”) (Wiktionary: مَشْي), used as an adverb.

funFacts: German zu Fuß and Greek με τα πόδια name the foot; Arabic says “walking” — or in full مَشْيًا عَلَى الْأَقْدَامِ, walking on the feet.
pitfalls: Unlike the vehicles (بِالْحَافِلَةِ, بِالسَّيَّارَةِ), “on foot” takes no بِـ: أَذْهَبُ مَشْيًا.
subtleties: -an is the accusative used as an adverb, as in مَسَاءً (in the evening) and شُكْرًا (thanks).

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Queues at the counter, a paper in the pocket.

examples.tr: I’d like a ticket to Alexandria.

examples.text: كَتَبْتُ تَذْكِرَةً صَغِيرَةً حَتَّى لَا أَنْسَى الْمَوْعِدَ.
examples.tr: I wrote a little note so as not to forget the appointment.

synonyms.nuance: card; also a ticket for an event or a boarding pass

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the verbal noun of ذَكَّرَ (form II, “to remind”) — “memorandum”, later “ticket”; root ذ ك ر (to remember).

funFacts: Literally “a reminder”: the same root gives ذِكْرَى (memory) and ذَكَرَ (to mention).
pitfalls: The plural تَذَاكِرُ is diptote (no tanwīn): تَذَاكِرُ كَثِيرَةٌ (Wiktionary also gives تَذْكِرَات).
Written with ذ; Egyptians say tazkara.
subtleties: تَذْكِرَتَانِ, two tickets: the dual — no number needed.
